title: Building JSON APIs
summary: Design a REST-style resource with the right methods and status codes, parse and validate JSON bodies, return consistent error shapes and call the API from Node with fetch.
introduction: Most Node servers exist to serve JSON to a front end, a mobile app or another service. The conventions that make such an API pleasant are small in number: resources named by URL, HTTP methods for the action, status codes that mean what they say, and one shape for every error. In this lesson you turn the bookshelf into a complete create-read-delete API with Express 5, validate what clients send, handle malformed JSON gracefully, and write a client with Node's built-in `fetch`.
learningObjectives: Map resources to URLs and actions to HTTP methods and status codes
Parse JSON bodies with express.json and validate the fields you receive
Return a consistent error shape and call the API from a Node script with fetch

blocks.text: A **resource** is a thing your API manages, named by a plural noun in the URL: `/api/books`, `/api/books/3`. The HTTP method says what to do with it, and the status code tells the client how it went, before it even reads the body.

rows: List books (filters go in the query string)
Create a book from the JSON body
Replace or partially update a book

blocks.text: Two more codes cover the client's mistakes: `400 Bad Request` when the body is missing or invalid, and `409 Conflict` when the request is valid but clashes with current state (a duplicate ISBN, for instance). Everything that is *your* fault is `500`.

`express.json()` is the middleware that reads a JSON body and puts the parsed object in `req.body`. It must be registered before the routes. The rest is the pattern from the previous lessons, applied to each row of the table above:

blocks.title: api.js

blocks.text: Start it with `node --watch api.js` and exercise every route. `-d` sends a body, `-H` sets the content type that `express.json()` looks for, and the `-w` format prints the status code of the `DELETE`, whose body is empty (on Windows, replace `/dev/null` with `NUL`):

blocks.code:
curl -s -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Snow Crash","author":"Neal Stephenson","year":1992}' http://localhost:3000/api/books
curl -s -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"author":"Nobody"}' http://localhost:3000/api/books
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X DELETE http://localhost:3000/api/books/2
curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/books

blocks.title: Terminal (one line per command)

blocks.text: Never assume the body has the shape you documented. The `POST` route checks that `title` is a non-empty string, supplies defaults for optional fields and ignores anything else the client sent, which also stops a client from choosing its own `id`. For bigger payloads, a schema library such as `zod` or `ajv` replaces the hand-written checks, but the response is the same: `400` with a message that tells the client what to fix.

blocks.title: req.body may be undefined
blocks.text: If the client forgets the `Content-Type: application/json` header, or sends no body at all, `express.json()` leaves `req.body` undefined in Express 5, and `const { title } = req.body` throws a `TypeError` that becomes a `500`. Destructure from `req.body ?? {}` so that a missing body turns into a clean `400` from your own validation instead.

Every error response above is `{ "error": "message" }`, so a client can handle them with one code path. The error middleware at the end extends this to failures you did not write a route for. When the body is not valid JSON, `express.json()` passes an error with `type === 'entity.parse.failed'` to the error handler; without that handler Express would reply with an HTML page, which breaks any client expecting JSON.

Node has the same `fetch` as the browser, so a script, a test or another service can talk to the API without extra packages. `response.json()` parses the body; check `response.status` or `response.ok` first, because `fetch` only rejects on network failure, never on a `4xx` or `5xx` status:

blocks.title: client.js
node client.js, against a freshly started api.js
blocks.content:
201 application/json; charset=utf-8
{ id: 3, title: 'Hyperion', author: 'Dan Simmons', year: 1989 }

blocks.title: Data that survives a restart
blocks.text: The `books` array lives in memory, so every restart resets it and two server processes would disagree. The [databases lesson](/tutorials/nodejs/databases) swaps the array for an SQLite table with the same routes.

questions.question: A client sends `POST /api/books` with a valid body and the server stores a new book. Which status code should the response use?
questions.explanation: 201 Created signals that a new resource now exists; the response body conventionally contains the created resource with its id.

questions.question: `await fetch(url)` rejects with an error when the server responds with status 404.
questions.explanation: fetch resolves for any HTTP response, including 4xx and 5xx; it only rejects on network-level failures. Check response.ok or response.status yourself.

seo.title: Build a JSON REST API with Node.js and Express 5
seo.description: Build a JSON API with Express 5: resources, HTTP methods and status codes, express.json, input validation, consistent error responses and a fetch client.
